title: Predictive plant biology from genome to whole-organism performance

concept.text: The innovation would be a reliable way to predict how a plant grows, functions and reproduces from its genetic variation, environmental history and specified interventions. It would connect DNA variation with gene regulation, development and physiology over time, allowing researchers to forecast the performance of genotypes they have not yet grown under the conditions being considered. These forecasts would need to capture genotype-by-environment interactions: the same genetic change can have different consequences in different environments or at different developmental stages.

Concept synthesis: the intended capability extends from predicting individual measured traits to predicting connected aspects of whole-organism performance, including development, physiological responses and reproductive outcomes. A useful system would state which genetic information, environmental observations and phenotypic measurements it requires, how far ahead it can predict, and where its uncertainty becomes too large for a decision. Regulation and environmental history belong to this broader proposed scope; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate that these components have already been integrated comprehensively.

significance.text: Reliable predictions across unfamiliar genotypes and environments could change how plant experiments and breeding programs are organized. Researchers could compare expected developmental trajectories before committing to long growth trials, identify informative measurement times and prioritize combinations of genotype and environment. The dynamicGP study connects prediction of time-resolved traits with understanding genetic effects on the changing plant phenome, providing a narrower demonstration relevant to this ambition.

Conditional significance synthesis: if the system also predicted responses to specified interventions, it could help compare competing biological explanations by testing whether their predicted outcomes differ and which agree with subsequent experiments. That would give botany a broadly useful instrument for prioritizing experiments and examining causal hypotheses. Predictive accuracy alone would not identify a unique causal mechanism: different explanations can produce similar forecasts, and intervention predictions would still require experimental validation.

Conditional downstream synthesis: sufficiently accurate predictions could support the design of crops suited to changing climates, the selection of useful genetic combinations and the assessment of tradeoffs between growth, stress responses and reproduction. Those benefits would depend on the environments, traits and interventions actually validated, as well as the cost of obtaining the required inputs. A successful model within several crop groups would not automatically become a universal simulator of plants or eliminate field trials.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is dependable transfer beyond the genetic populations and environmental conditions represented in model development. A model can learn useful associations within a dataset without retaining accuracy when genetic backgrounds, developmental conditions or environmental exposures change. The dynamicGP article explicitly identifies transferability across populations and environments as a limitation inherited from genomic prediction. Its discussion also leaves extensions involving environmental factors and relationships to agronomic phenotypes for future work.

Scientific synthesis: achieving the broader goal requires connecting processes that operate at different scales and times. Genetic and regulatory differences influence cell behavior and tissue development; these affect plant form and physiology; environmental exposures alter these relationships throughout the life cycle. The engineering challenge is to represent enough of these dependencies to predict consequential outcomes while keeping measurements and computation practical. It also requires distinguishing a forecast that follows familiar correlations from one that remains reliable when an intervention changes the relationships on which those correlations depended.

Evaluation synthesis: another barrier is knowing when the model should be trusted. Genetic novelty, environmental novelty, forecast length and the availability of early phenotypic measurements can each change the difficulty of prediction. Models therefore need uncertainty estimates that remain informative under the declared forms of novelty. Developmental and physiological predictions must also be connected to reproductive outcomes; accurate forecasts of visible morphology alone would not establish accurate forecasts of whole-plant performance.

current_state.text: On 17 April 2025, Hobby and colleagues published “Predicting plant trait dynamics from genetic markers,” describing dynamicGP. Using genetic markers and high-throughput phenotyping data from a maize multiparent advanced generation inter-cross population and an Arabidopsis thaliana diversity panel, the study predicted time-dependent morphometric, geometric and colourimetric traits. It reported better performance than the tested ridge-regression best linear unbiased prediction, or RR-BLUP, baselines in aggregate comparisons. This supports a specific advance in predicting trait dynamics; it does not establish superiority over every statistical or process-based alternative.

The phenotypic inputs are essential to interpreting that achievement. In the iterative version of dynamicGP, measured trait values at each timepoint were used to predict the following timepoint. The recursive version began with an initial phenotypic measurement and then continued prediction recursively. The demonstrated capability therefore used genetic markers together with phenotypic observations. It was not a demonstration of predicting an entire life cycle from DNA alone, general causal responses to interventions, or reproductive performance across unfamiliar species and environments.

The supplied review assessed retained full article text containing Results, Discussion and Methods, which supersedes the earlier account that the Nature assessment depended only on an accessible article description after a sign-in redirect. That review did not independently inspect linked supplements or figure images. Some pages in the separately retained PDF lacked extractable text, but the full HTML text supported the findings summarized here. These access boundaries limit further interpretation of figures and supplementary analyses without negating the textually documented results.

The research notes also identify a source attributed to Pauli and colleagues, “Digital twins for plant and crop improvement,” dated 8 July 2026, with DOI 10.1016/j.tplants.2026.06.005. However, the supplied review found only a cookie challenge in the retained PubMed content, with no article identity or abstract available for assessment. Consequently, the attributed discussion of digital-twin promise and scalability cannot be treated here as verified scientific evidence. This is an access limitation, not evidence that the publication or its attributed claims are false.

Evidence-scope synthesis: the supplied material establishes the April 2025 dynamicGP demonstration and its stated boundaries. It does not establish the latest state of the entire field as of 1 November 2026, because no bounded search results were supplied. The broader innovation remains a proposed capability in this record; the evidence does not demonstrate its completion or justify a comprehensive claim that every component remains unsolved by every approach.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: prospectively predict development, physiology and reproductive performance for unseen genotypes in predeclared unfamiliar environments and under specified interventions. Before outcomes are observed, define the degree of genetic and environmental novelty, intervention classes, endpoints, prediction horizons and practically useful accuracy thresholds. Specify exactly which phenotypic measurements are permitted at prediction time, distinguishing forecasts based on initial observations from those updated with repeated measurements. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established field standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed comparative evaluation: test against strong statistical and process-based models given comparable information. Report performance across the declared traits, environments, genetic groups and forecast horizons, alongside aggregate results, so that success in easier cases does not conceal important failures. Evaluate whether uncertainty estimates match observed errors and whether they identify cases in which the system cannot make a useful prediction. A practical demonstration should also account for the measurement burden needed to achieve its reported accuracy.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed comparative evaluation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope: independent teams should replicate the prospective results across several plant families using sufficiently documented data, model versions and evaluation procedures. Intervention tests should examine whether predicted changes occur, while mechanistic conclusions should remain limited to what those experiments distinguish. Success would establish completion within the declared genetic, environmental and intervention scope. Any finite set of trials demonstrates breadth across tested cases, rather than literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and scope

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison: genomic prediction supplies a direct foundation by relating genetic markers to traits; systems biology offers ways to connect interacting biological processes; process-based crop models represent growth and physiological responses; and plant digital twins provide a related framework for an evolving model tied to observations. BOT-05 would overlap with all four but would be defined by demonstrated prospective prediction across its declared scope. Calling a system a digital twin would not by itself establish that capability.

Roster comparison: BOT-03, “Whole-plant synthetic genome construction and rewriting,” and BOT-04, “An inexpensive, broadly transferable method to edit and regenerate plants,” concern constructing or modifying plants. BOT-05 concerns predicting the consequences of genetic and environmental differences. Editing and genome rewriting could supply interventions for testing predictions, while predictive models could help prioritize modifications. Each construction capability remains distinct from the ability to forecast resulting organismal performance.

Roster comparison: BOT-12, “A causal map of plant-wide communication and plasmodesmatal control,” BOT-13, “A predictive mechanism for plant cell-wall growth and mechanical sensing,” and BOT-17, “Predictive control of plant cell-division planes and tissue patterning,” address mechanisms that could contribute to whole-plant models. BOT-14, “Programmable, multigenerational epigenetic inheritance of adaptive plant traits,” adds inherited regulatory effects and a multigenerational horizon. BOT-05 would need to represent such processes where they materially affect its forecasts, but success at integrated prediction would not automatically resolve each mechanism or establish control over it.

Roster comparison: BOT-01, “Nitrogen-fixing partnerships for major cereal crops,” and BOT-16, “Predictable control of plant–mycorrhizal nutrient exchange,” concern biological partnerships that influence nutrient supply. BOT-02, “A functional carbon-concentrating photosynthetic system in rice,” concerns a specific photosynthetic capability, while BOT-10, “Plants that reliably deposit durable additional carbon in soil,” concerns a plant–soil carbon outcome. BOT-05 could help assess their consequences for growth and reproduction, but organismal prediction would not itself establish functional nitrogen fixation, nutrient-exchange control, a carbon-concentrating system or durable additional soil carbon.

Roster comparison: BOT-06, “Reliable clonal seed reproduction across major crop families,” BOT-07, “Transferable resurrection-like desiccation tolerance in productive crops,” BOT-08, “Programmable, durable plant immunity against diverse pathogens,” and BOT-15, “Broadly transferable perennial grain production,” concern particular reproductive, stress-response, immune or life-history capabilities. They offer demanding applications and intervention tests for BOT-05, especially where a useful trait changes other aspects of performance. Predicting those tradeoffs would remain distinct from engineering the traits or proving their durability and transferability.

Roster comparison: BOT-09, “Affordable preservation and recovery of exceptional plant diversity,” could preserve biological material useful for testing predictive breadth, but concerns preservation and recovery rather than performance forecasting. BOT-11, “A testable causal explanation for the early radiation of flowering plants,” concerns a historical evolutionary explanation. Predictive plant models might help examine consequences of proposed mechanisms, but successful forecasts of living plants would not by themselves establish why an ancient radiation occurred.

change_log.change: Preserved BOT-05 and its title while expanding the concept into an explicit prospective prediction goal spanning development, physiology, reproduction and environmental history.
change_log.reason: The research and review describe a coherent innovation whose identity is broader than the demonstrated dynamicGP result.

change_log.change: Replaced the earlier Nature access account with the review's assessment of retained full article text, while preserving the limits concerning figures, supplements and PDF extraction.
change_log.reason: The supplied review documents Results, Discussion and Methods in the retained HTML; the earlier description of reliance only on an accessible article description was superseded.

change_log.change: Specified the April 2025 dynamicGP populations, trait categories, tested RR-BLUP comparisons and required phenotypic measurements.
change_log.reason: These details distinguish the demonstrated advance from genome-only forecasting and prevent a particular baseline comparison from becoming a claim of general superiority.

change_log.change: Separated the documented dynamicGP achievement from general intervention prediction, reproductive-performance forecasting and transfer across unfamiliar species or environments.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports the narrower achievement and explicitly identifies transferability limitations.

change_log.change: Qualified the Pauli citation and removed its attributed scientific discussion as established evidence.
change_log.reason: The retained PubMed artifact contains only a cookie challenge, so its identity and abstract content could not be assessed. Missing access does not establish falsity.

change_log.change: Preserved the conditional significance while distinguishing comparison of causal explanations from identification of a unique causal mechanism.
change_log.reason: Predictive success can discriminate between different expected outcomes without uniquely establishing the mechanism responsible.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed completion criteria to include declared novelty, permitted inputs, endpoints, horizons, useful accuracy, uncertainty, comparable baselines and independent replication.
change_log.reason: The review identified these as necessary specifications for an assessable proposal, while emphasizing that they are not established standards and cannot prove universality.

change_log.change: Added explicit distinctions and potential connections for every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Related enabling methods, mechanistic goals and application traits overlap with BOT-05 without being merged into its completion claim.

change_log.change: Limited the temporal conclusion to what the supplied evidence establishes.
change_log.reason: No bounded search results were supplied to establish field-wide freshness as of 1 November 2026.

unresolved_issues: The latest field-wide state as of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved; the supplied record contains no bounded search results.
The identity, publication details and scientific content attributed to the Pauli source remain unverified from the retained cookie-challenge artifact.

The proposed capability still needs operational definitions of genetic and environmental novelty, intervention classes, permitted phenotypic inputs, endpoints, prediction horizons and useful accuracy thresholds.
The record does not establish how much performance depends on repeated phenotypic measurements versus an initial observation under matched evaluation conditions.

The supplied review did not independently inspect figure images or linked supplements, and some retained PDF pages lacked extractable text; claims requiring those materials remain outside this synthesis.
No quantitative effect sizes for dynamicGP's improvement over the tested baselines are supplied in the review, so the magnitude of improvement is not specified.

prerequisites.reason: BOT-05 uses predictions of how genetic changes affect biological outcomes across plant contexts to connect genome variation to whole-plant performance.
BOT-05 uses predictions of regulatory-sequence effects to connect plant genetic variation to organismal performance.
BOT-05 uses predictions of context-dependent genetic interactions to forecast whole-plant performance.
